Jesus called a little child to himself, and set him in the middle of them,
and said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven.
Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me,
b: In this passage the disciples ask a question about rank and greatness in the Kingdom of Heaven: "Who is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?" This shows that their understanding of the Kingdom still carried earthly ideas of power and position. Jesus' answer is both profound and challenging: He calls a little child to stand among them, making the child a symbol of the truth of the Kingdom and the center of His teaching.

Jesus says, "Unless you turn and become like little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven." Here "turn" means a thorough change of mindset and heart: giving up adult pride and competition, and learning the humility and innocence of a child. Jesus goes on to explain that greatness in the Kingdom is built on humility, and whoever humbles himself like a little child will be counted greatest in the Kingdom.

Jesus' words also point to a spirit of welcome and service in the life of faith: "Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me." This is not only an attitude toward children, but a welcome for all humble seekers, reflecting the heart of service and love that Christians should have.

Through this passage God reminds us that in His Kingdom true greatness comes from humility and service. He encourages us to cast aside worldly competition and self-promotion, and to pursue instead a pure and selfless way of life, relying on and worshiping Him with childlike faith.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, help us learn the humility and trust of little children, so that in our lives we may lay down prejudice and pride and treat others with open and welcoming hearts. Teach us to grow in Your love and become people who may be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven. In this process, give us wisdom and strength, so that we may live out Your example and influence the world around us with humility and love. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Think back: do I sometimes emphasize self too much and neglect the spirit of humility and service? Consider how you can show more humility in daily life and come to God with childlike faith.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck, and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea.
“Woe to the world because of occasions of stumbling! For it must be that the occasions come, but woe to that person through whom the occasion comes!

If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off, and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life maimed or crippled, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into the eternal fire.
If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out, and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into the Gehenna of fire.
See that you don’t despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.
b: In this passage Jesus teaches us to be extremely careful in how we treat the young and vulnerable in the faith. He warns that anyone who causes one of "these little ones" to stumble faces a terrible outcome: a great millstone hung around the neck and a drowning in the depths of the sea, a stark picture of how grave such wrongdoing is. Jesus then turns to our own lives and stresses the importance of not stumbling ourselves, even suggesting that we give up a part of the body rather than lose the soul forever. Entering the Kingdom of God matters more than anything in this world.

Jesus' teaching stresses personal responsibility, and it also reminds us of the worth of every believer, especially those who may seem unnoticed or insignificant. He tells us that their angels in heaven always see the face of His Father, which means these little ones are specially watched over and cared for by God.

Through this passage God reminds us that our actions and decisions affect not only ourselves but also, deeply, the people around us, especially those who depend on our guidance and protection in faith and in life. We are called to act with the love and wisdom of Christ, and never to become a stumbling block on someone else's spiritual path.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through Your word to treat our brothers and sisters in the faith with great care and thoughtfulness. Give us wisdom and love, so that we not only avoid causing anyone to stumble but also hold one another up in Your love. Help us see the value of every person in Your eyes, so that our lives may bear witness to Your glory. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Consider whether there is anything in your life that may unintentionally cause one of these "little ones" to stumble. How can you guard your words and actions so that they better reflect the love and righteousness of Christ?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost.
“What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray?
If he finds it, most certainly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray.
Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the lost sheep to show us God's deep concern for every soul. Even when only one sheep goes astray, the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine that are safe and goes to look for the one that is lost. When he finds it, his joy over that one sheep is greater than his joy over the ninety-nine that never wandered. This teaches us that God's saving love for every person is full of tenderness and patience.

Jesus makes it clear that it is not the will of our Father in heaven that one of these little ones should perish. This is not only a lesson about God's love, but also a challenge to us: in our daily lives and ministry, do we show the same heart in seeking out and restoring those who have lost their way spiritually?

Through this passage God reminds us that His plan of salvation is wide and welcoming, and that no one is unimportant. We are called to reflect this seeking heart, not only in spiritual matters but also in the way we serve the people around us every day.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through the parable of the lost sheep how deeply You love every person. Give us the same heart to seek out and care for those who have lost their way on life's journey. Help us welcome everyone with love, and show Your love and compassion in our words and actions. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Is there someone in your circle who is struggling or wandering spiritually? How can you be a guide and a support to help them find their way home?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.
b: In this passage Jesus teaches us how to deal with conflict and wrongdoing among believers. First, if your brother sins against you, go and talk to him privately. This protects his dignity and gives reconciliation a space free from outside interference. If that conversation does not settle the matter, the second step is to take one or two others along as witnesses, so that the process is fair and open. If that still does not work, the matter is brought to the church, the wider community of faith. And if the person refuses even the church's counsel, he is to be treated as an outsider, which shows how seriously the community takes persistent wrongdoing.

Through this passage God shows us that He wants us to practice forgiveness and reconciliation in our relationships. He gives us wisdom and humility to handle disputes with one another, and He urges us to act in love and truth so that the Christian community stays united and pure.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word how to deal with conflict and wrongdoing. Give us wisdom and a humble heart, so that we may handle every relational dispute with the love of Christ and seek true reconciliation and restoration. Help us be peacemakers, and put Your teaching into practice in our church and community. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Think back: how do you usually react when you are in conflict with someone? How can you follow the teaching of Matthew 18 more faithfully, and so promote reconciliation and a spirit of love?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.
Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”
b: This passage explores authority and the power of unity in the Christian community. Jesus stresses that the keys of the Kingdom have been entrusted to the church, which means that spiritual decisions made on earth are reflected in heaven. This includes the exercise of authority in church discipline and forgiveness, and it reminds us that our actions and decisions should be in line with the Father's will.

Jesus goes on to say that when believers agree together on earth about anything they ask, His Father in heaven will do it for them. This highlights the importance of unity and the power of acting together in faith.

Finally, Jesus assures us that wherever two or three gather in His name, He is there among them. This emphasizes the sacredness of the church and the importance of every gathering, no matter how large or small.

Through this passage God reminds us that the responsibility we carry as His people is great. Every gathering and every prayer made in unity is valued by God, and each is an opportunity to exercise heaven's authority. God encourages us to act carefully in our faith and always to seek His heart, so that our decisions agree with His will.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word how powerful our unity and prayer are in Your Kingdom. Help us treasure and use well the authority You have given us, binding and loosing with humble and obedient hearts. Make us aware of Your presence every time we gather, and help us seek Your face in everything. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: How do you practice unity with other believers in daily life? Have you ever seen God keep His promise in answer to prayer made together in your church or small group?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who wanted to reconcile accounts with his servants.
When he had begun to reconcile, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.
But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’
The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt.
“But that servant went out, and found one of his fellow servants, who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him, and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’
“So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’
He would not, but went and cast him into prison, until he should pay back that which was due.
So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
Then his lord called him in, and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt, because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors, until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”
b: In this passage Peter asks Jesus how many times he should forgive a brother who sins against him. Jesus not only raises the number to "seventy times seven" but also tells a parable to show how important unconditional forgiveness is. In the parable a king forgives his servant an enormous debt, yet that servant does not show the same mercy to his fellow servant. The story reveals the serious consequences of lacking mercy toward others.

Jesus' teaching shows that forgiveness is important not only on a religious level but also as the foundation of harmony in our relationships. Forgiveness is not a matter of counting; it is an attitude of heart, a willingness to keep releasing others from their offenses. The parable teaches us that the Father's forgiveness of us is unconditional, and that we should follow His example by forgiving unconditionally.

Through this passage God reminds us to forgive from the heart those who wrong us. This is not only because we ourselves need forgiveness, but because it is the way to live out the true nature of Christian love and compassion.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through Your word how wide and deep Your forgiveness of us is. Help us learn to forgive as You forgive, continuing to release others even when we are hurt again and again. Give us a generous heart, so that we not only seek our own reconciliation but also become a bridge to reconciliation for others. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Think back: is there someone you have not yet forgiven from the bottom of your heart? How is holding on to this affecting your spiritual life? What step can you take to practice real forgiveness, as Jesus taught?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee, and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.
Great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there.
Pharisees came to him, testing him, and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”
He answered, “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female,
and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?’
So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.”
They asked him, “Why then did Moses command us to give her a certificate of divorce, and divorce her?”
He said to them, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so.
I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her when she is divorced commits adultery.”
His disciples said to him, “If this is the case of the man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.”
But he said to them, “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given.

For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”
b: In this passage Jesus speaks about the sacredness of marriage and the question of divorce. When the Pharisees ask whether it is lawful to divorce a wife for any reason, Jesus goes back to Genesis and affirms that marriage was established by God, a covenant in which a man and a woman become one flesh before Him, and it should not be casually broken. Jesus points out that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of people's hearts, but that this was not God's original intention. He adds that, except for sexual immorality, remarriage after divorce amounts to adultery.

Jesus' teaching challenged the social norms of the day and the Pharisees' interpretation, and it highlights the permanence and sacredness of marriage. His answer was not only a reply to a question of that time but also gives us today a holy way of looking at the marriage relationship.

Through this passage God reminds us that marriage is a holy covenant He established, and it should be honored and protected. When we face difficulties in marriage, we should seek God's wisdom and guidance and work to resolve our differences, rather than look for a way to escape our responsibility.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word how important and sacred marriage is. Help us treasure and protect every marriage You have given, so that in hard times we seek Your face and support one another in love and faithfulness. Give us wisdom and grace, so that our families may honor Your name. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Consider whether your view of marriage agrees with Jesus' teaching. How are you putting Jesus' call to faithful, lasting commitment into practice in your relationships? How can you show obedience to God's will more fully in your marriage or relationships?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then little children were brought to him, that he should lay his hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them.
But Jesus said, “Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these.”
He laid his hands on them, and departed from there.
b: This passage records Jesus welcoming and blessing little children, and it reveals the nature of the Kingdom of Heaven. When children were brought to Jesus, the disciples at first rebuked those who brought them, probably thinking they would trouble Him. But Jesus responded with love and welcome. He not only received the children but also declared, "For the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to such as these."

Jesus is showing that the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to people who are like little children: pure in heart, humble, and dependent. The natural trust and openness of children is the attitude every believer should pursue. In the adult world such qualities are often seen as weaknesses, but in Jesus' teaching they are the key to entering the Kingdom.

Through this passage God reminds us to pursue purity of heart and humility, and to remain fully dependent on Him. This is the attitude every believer should seek, especially when facing life's challenges and decisions.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through the teaching of Jesus Christ to come to You like little children. Give us a pure and humble heart, so that we keep depending on You in daily life and measure our actions and attitudes by Your standard. Help us keep a childlike faith in every circumstance and show the true character of the Kingdom of Heaven. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: In your daily life, how do you keep a childlike faith and sincerity? How do you practice humility and dependence on God in your relationships?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”
He said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
He said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “ ‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’
‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ ”
The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”
But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.
b: In this passage a rich young man comes to Jesus and asks how he can have eternal life. His question shows his longing for eternal life, but it also exposes a misunderstanding of how to reach it: he thinks he can gain it by doing good deeds. Jesus first challenges his idea of "good," stressing that only God is truly good. Then Jesus lists commandments that must be kept: do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not give false testimony, and love your neighbor as yourself, which are basic moral laws.

When the young man confidently replies that he has kept all these, Jesus points to what is holding his heart: his wealth. Jesus tells him that if he wants to be complete, he must sell what he owns, give to the poor, and follow Jesus. These words reveal the cost of following Jesus and test how attached the young man is to material wealth. Faced with this challenge, the young man went away sad, because he could not let go of his riches.

Through this passage God reminds us that truly following Him is not just outwardly keeping laws and rules but an inner transformation, which requires us to let go of everything that may hinder our relationship with God. Jesus calls us to put the Kingdom of God first, and that may mean giving up the things and the status we treasure most.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Jesus Christ the depth and the sacrifice that following You requires. Help us recognize and let go of whatever keeps us from depending on You with our whole heart. Give us courage and strength to place You at the center of our lives and to live the life You call us to. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: What in your life may be like the young man's wealth, an obstacle to following Jesus? How can you place these things more fully in God's hands and follow Him wholeheartedly?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty.
Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?”
Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
Then Peter answered, “Behold, we have left everything, and followed you. What then will we have?”

Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive one hundred times, and will inherit eternal life.
But many will be last who are first; and first who are last.
b: In this passage Jesus reveals deeply how wealth affects the spiritual life. He tells His disciples that it is very hard for a rich person to enter the Kingdom of Heaven, and He says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye. The disciples are astonished and ask, "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answers that with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. His words stress that salvation is God's work, and no one can reach it by their own strength or riches.

When Peter says that they have left everything to follow Jesus and asks what they will have, Jesus gives a promise: at the renewal of all things, those who follow Him will sit with Him on thrones of glory and inherit eternal life. Jesus stresses that everyone who has left homes and possessions for His name's sake will receive a hundred times as much in the Kingdom.

The core message of this passage is that spiritual promises and eternal values far outweigh worldly wealth. Jesus challenges His disciples, and us today, to rethink our dependence on wealth and our pursuit of it, and encourages us to put our trust in God's power and promises.

Through this passage God reminds us that true security and worth come not from what we own but from following Jesus and seeking heavenly treasure. He encourages us to believe that in His Kingdom, giving up everything and making sacrifices for the sake of seeking God's Kingdom will receive an eternal reward.
q: How much of my thought and energy goes into pursuing material wealth? Is this affecting my pursuit of God's Kingdom? How can I readjust my focus to pursue spiritual treasure more?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for helping us understand through Jesus Christ that true value is not in the wealth of this world but in seeking Your Kingdom and Your righteousness. Help us be freed from worldly chains and rely on You with our whole heart, answering Your call on our lives with faith and obedience. In times of temptation and challenge, remind us that You are the source of all that is possible. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “For the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who was the master of a household, who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.
When he had agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
He went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace.
He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you.’ So they went their way.
Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did likewise.
About the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle. He said to them, ‘Why do you stand here all day idle?’
“They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ “He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and you will receive whatever is right.’
When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first.’
“When those who were hired at about the eleventh hour came, they each received a denarius.
When the first came, they supposed that they would receive more; and they likewise each received a denarius.
When they received it, they murmured against the master of the household,
saying, ‘These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!’
“But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree with me for a denarius?
Take that which is yours, and go your way. It is my desire to give to this last just as much as to you.
Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’
So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of a landowner hiring workers for his vineyard to show us the principles of the Kingdom of Heaven, especially the display of justice and grace. Whether the workers began in the morning or near evening, the landowner gave them all the same wage, a denarius. This shows that God's grace goes beyond our ordinary ideas of fairness.

The landowner's actions challenge those workers who thought they deserved more because they had worked more. The story stresses that God's grace is generous, and He has every right to reward each person as He sees fit. It reflects that God's invitation to all believers is fair, no matter at what stage of life a person responds to His call.

Through this passage God reveals to us that His Kingdom does not follow the world's standards of evaluation. In the Kingdom of Heaven, when people lose their thankfulness and begin to count their own gains and losses, the last will become first and the first last. God's grace is given to each person not on the basis of their effort or seniority but on the basis of His unconditional love and generosity.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us the principles of Your Kingdom through this parable. Help us understand Your generous grace, and learn to see justice and reward through Your eyes. Keep us from counting personal gains and losses, and let us focus on serving faithfully in Your Kingdom. Make our hearts more like Yours, to embrace and live out this unconditional love and acceptance. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: Have you ever been dissatisfied because you compared your gains with those of others? How can you apply this parable to your personal faith and your service in the church, so as to reflect God's generous grace more fully?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them,
“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death,
and will hand him over to the Gentiles to mock, to scourge, and to crucify; and the third day he will be raised up.”
b: In this passage Jesus clearly foretells His suffering and resurrection. On the way up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the disciples aside privately and reveals what is about to happen. He says He will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes and condemned to death. This shows that Jesus knew His destiny clearly and held to it firmly, and it also stresses His complete obedience to the Father's will.

Jesus' prophecy says He will be handed over to the Gentiles, to be mocked, flogged, and finally crucified. All these events point to His sacrifice, paying the price for the sins of all humanity. Yet Jesus' words do not stop at the suffering: He declares clearly that after all this He will be raised up on the third day. This prophecy establishes the core of the Christian faith, Jesus' death and resurrection, and it is the foundation of every believer's salvation.

Through this passage God shows us the perfection of His sovereignty and plan. Though the road was hard, He still led Jesus to the cross to finish the work of redemption. He reminds us that whatever trial or hardship we face, God's will is always accomplished, and His glory is revealed through these very processes.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Your plan of redemption through the suffering and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Give us faith to trust that Your plan is perfect even when we face hardship and challenge in life. Help us learn to depend on You in every circumstance and to find peace in Your will. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: When you face challenges and uncertainty in life, how do you find strength to rely on God's plan? How do you understand and accept that God has His purpose and plan even in suffering?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, kneeling and asking a certain thing of him.
He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand, and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom.”

But Jesus answered, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?” They said to him, “We are able.”

He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with, but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give; but it is for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”
When the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers.
b: In this passage the mother of the sons of Zebedee makes a bold request of Jesus: that her two sons may sit, one on His right hand and one on His left, in His Kingdom. This shows that she recognized Jesus' kingship, but it also shows a misunderstanding of the deeper meaning of His mission.

Jesus' reply is deep and revealing. He asks whether her sons are ready to share the same suffering He will bear, that is, "to drink the cup that I am about to drink." Here the "cup" symbolizes the suffering and sacrifice Jesus was about to undergo. Jesus goes on to make clear that the places at His right and left are not decided by human desire but are for those for whom they have been prepared by His Father.

This passage teaches us that following Jesus is not merely a search for glory and high position; more importantly, it means being ready to share the suffering and trials that Jesus went through. Jesus stresses that God's Kingdom is not built on worldly power and status but on service, sacrifice, and obedience to God's will.

Through this passage God reminds us that true greatness comes from serving others and giving up ourselves. In God's Kingdom the highest honor is to lay ourselves down for God's glory and the good of others.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Son Jesus Christ what true greatness is. Help us learn humility and seek to serve and sacrifice in daily life rather than seek power and position. When we face trials and suffering, give us strength to endure to the end and bring glory to Your Kingdom. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: What does "drinking the cup that Jesus drank" mean in your life? As you pursue your personal ambitions, how do you balance them with a spirit of service and self-sacrifice?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But Jesus summoned them, and said, “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant,
even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
b: In this passage Jesus explains to His disciples the true nature of leadership and greatness. While the disciples were arguing about who should hold the highest place in Jesus' Kingdom, Jesus turned their traditional view of power and position upside down. He points out that the rulers of the world often lead others through power and control, but in God's Kingdom whoever wants to be great must be a servant.

Jesus' own life and ministry are the ultimate example of service and sacrifice. He says that He came into the world not to be served but to serve, and even to give His life as a ransom. This is the heart of Christian leadership: not seeking personal advancement but committing to service and sacrifice for the good of others.

Through this passage God reminds us that in His eyes true greatness and leadership do not come from exercising power but from how we serve others. This calls us to overturn our usual way of thinking and to see leadership as an opportunity for service and devotion.
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your Son Jesus Christ what true service and leadership are. Help us learn humility, to lead with a servant's heart, and in daily life to look for chances to serve others rather than to be served. Give us a heart willing to sacrifice ourselves to help others, so that we may walk in Your love and be Your faithful servants. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen. [Reflection question]: In your daily life, what opportunities are there to turn leadership into service? How do you understand "giving His life as a ransom for many" in practical terms in today's society?
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.
Behold, two blind men sitting by the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!”
The multitude rebuked them, telling them that they should be quiet, but they cried out even more, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!”
Jesus stood still, and called them, and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They told him, “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.”
Jesus, being moved with compassion, touched their eyes; and immediately their eyes received their sight, and they followed him.
b: This passage describes Jesus meeting two blind men as He left Jericho. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out loudly for His mercy, in spite of the crowd's attempts to silence and rebuke them, showing their faith in Him and their urgent need. Jesus responded with compassion: He stopped, listened to their request, asked what they wanted Him to do for them, and then, moved with compassion, restored their sight.

This passage shows us several important lessons. First, no matter how much opposition or pressure we face from outside, we should keep seeking Jesus and expressing our trust in Him and our need of Him. Second, Jesus always responds with love and grace to those who sincerely seek Him. Finally, the story reminds us that Jesus' healing is not only the restoration of the body but also a spiritual awakening.
q: Think back: when in your life have you sought Jesus as urgently as these two blind men? When you faced obstacles and opposition, what kept you going in faith?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us unconditional love and compassion through Your Son Jesus Christ. Help us keep seeking You in difficulties and challenges, and increase our confidence in and dependence on Your word. Teach us, like these two blind men, to ignore the voices around us and focus on seeking Your face. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When they came near to Jerusalem, and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples,
saying to them, “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them, and bring them to me.
If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and immediately he will send them.”
All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying,
“Tell the daughter of Zion, behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”
The disciples went, and did just as Jesus commanded them,
and brought the donkey and the colt, and laid their clothes on them; and he sat on them.
A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road. Others cut branches from the trees, and spread them on the road.
The multitudes who went in front of him, and those who followed, kept shouting, “Hosanna  to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”
When he had come into Jerusalem, all the city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?”
The multitudes said, “This is the prophet, Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.”
b: This passage describes Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, commonly called "Palm Sunday." Jesus tells His disciples to go to the village ahead, find a donkey tied with her colt, and use "The Lord needs them" as the word to get permission. This shows Jesus' supernatural command of the situation, and it fulfills the prophecy of Zechariah, stressing His identity as a humble King.

As Jesus rode into the city on the donkey, the crowd responded enthusiastically. They spread their cloaks and branches on the road to welcome Him and shouted loudly that He is the "Son of David," expressing their recognition of Him as King. This scene is the climax of Jesus' public ministry and also foreshadows the beginning of His suffering.

From this passage God reminds us that Jesus is a King unlike what the world expects. His kingship is not built on force or political power but on humility, service, and sacrifice. His entry into the city was both a king's entrance and a symbol of self-sacrifice, foreshadowing His death for the redemption of all people.
q: How do you practice humility and service in your own life? When you face decisions that call you to set aside your own interests, how do you respond?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Your Son Jesus Christ what a true King is. Help us learn Jesus' humility and service and live out His example in our lives. When we face challenges and trials, let us remember that true strength comes from serving others and sacrificing ourselves. We ask all this in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus entered into the temple of God, and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves.
He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers!”
The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the son of David!” they were indignant,
and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of babes and nursing babies you have perfected praise?’ ”
He left them, and went out of the city to Bethany, and camped there.
b: This passage records Jesus cleansing the temple, showing His strong opposition to the commercialization of God's house by the religious leaders of the day. Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem and found people buying and selling there, turning a holy place meant for prayer into a marketplace for profit. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who sold doves, and rebuked them with the words of the prophet Isaiah: "My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers."

This act was not only a condemnation of the conduct of the religious leaders and merchants of that time; it is also a reminder to all believers that God's house, and our own lives, should be a place of prayer and spiritual seeking, not a center of other worldly activities.

In addition, Jesus healed the blind and the lame in the temple, showing His compassion for people and His power to heal, and further stressing the importance of the temple as a place of healing and restoration. The children shouting in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" reveal that even amid opposition from those in authority, the voice of truth and praise will still be heard.

From this passage God, through Jesus' actions, reminds us that our lives and our churches should focus on holy purposes and not be swayed by secular interests. By clearing out the buying and selling in the temple, Jesus calls us back to the purity and essence of the life of faith.
q: In your life, which areas or activities may have drifted away from a God-centered purpose? What can you do in practical terms to keep your heart and your living space clean, focused on God's will and on prayer?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us, through Jesus Christ's cleansing of the temple, to keep our lives and our churches pure and holy. Help us build our lives, personally and together, on prayer and on seeking You, and keep far from everything that may defile us or divide our devotion to You. Give us courage and wisdom, so that our lives become a testimony of continual worship and praise of You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry.
Seeing a fig tree by the road, he came to it, and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “Let there be no fruit from you forever!” Immediately the fig tree withered away.
When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree immediately wither away?”

Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, if you have faith, and don’t doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you told this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it would be done.
All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”
b: This passage tells of Jesus' remarkable action toward a fig tree and the teaching that follows. When Jesus was hungry, He came to a fig tree that was full of leaves but had no fruit. He spoke to the tree and told it that no fruit would ever grow on it again, and the tree withered at once. The disciples were amazed and asked how the fig tree withered so quickly.

Jesus' answer stresses the power of faith. He told the disciples that if they have faith and do not doubt, they will be able to do not only what was done to the fig tree but even say to a mountain that it be removed. This teaches us that the power of faith is immense and can make the impossible possible.

Jesus' words highlight the deep connection between prayer and faith: "All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive." This reminds us that when we trust and depend on God completely, our prayers can accomplish great things.

The lesson of this passage is not only about the power of faith but also a warning against formalism. Like the fig tree, leafy on the outside but without fruit, the life of faith needs to go beyond outward religious acts and bear real spiritual fruit.
q: In which areas of your life do you need to rely more on faith than on sight? How can you strengthen your faith in prayer?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us the importance of faith through Jesus' action with the fig tree. Strengthen our faith, so that when we face challenges and difficulties we do not doubt but are sure that You will answer our prayers. Help us pursue not only the outward form of faith but also bear abundant spiritual fruit in our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?”
Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, which if you tell me, I likewise will tell you by what authority I do these things.
The baptism of John, where was it from? From heaven or from men?” They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will ask us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From men,’ we fear the multitude, for all hold John as a prophet.”
They answered Jesus, and said, “We don’t know.” He also said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.
b: In this passage, as Jesus was teaching in the temple in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the people came and questioned His authority. They asked Him, "By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?" This was not only a challenge to Jesus' authority but also a strategy to make Him lose credibility in front of the people.

Jesus answered their question with a question of His own: where did John's baptism come from, from heaven or from men? This put the questioners in a difficult position, because whatever they answered would expose their motives and their inconsistency. In the end they chose to answer, "We don't know." So Jesus also refused to tell them by what authority He did these things.

This passage reveals Jesus' wisdom in responding to those who challenged Him. By asking a question, He let His opponents reveal their own hypocrisy and fear. In this way He kept the legitimacy of His actions while exposing the moral and spiritual failings of the religious leaders.

Through this passage God shows us the power of truth and the certain victory of righteousness, even in the face of power and challenge. Jesus teaches us to meet challenges with wisdom and firmness, and to stand firm in our faith.
q: When your faith and authority are questioned, how do you usually respond? How can you use Jesus' wisdom and calm to improve the way you respond?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Your Son Jesus Christ how to face challenges and questioning with wisdom and courage. Give us wisdom to tell true from false, and help us act with firm faith and a sense of justice when we meet difficulties in life. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first, and said, ‘Son, go work today in my vineyard.’
He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind, and went.
He came to the second, and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I’m going, sir,’ but he didn’t go.

Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you.

For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you didn’t believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. When you saw it, you didn’t even repent afterward, that you might believe him.
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable to teach the importance of obedience and true repentance. The parable is about a father and his two sons. The father asks them to go and work in the vineyard. The first son refuses at first, but later regrets it and obeys his father's command. The second son says with his mouth that he will go, but in the end does not keep his promise.

Through this story Jesus asks His listeners a question: which of the two sons really did the will of his father? The answer is the first, who, though he refused at first, changed his mind later and acted. This teaches us that even if we refuse at first to obey God, those who regret it and turn to God can still be accepted by Him.

Jesus goes on to say that the tax collectors and prostitutes, people often despised by society, entered God's Kingdom because they believed John's teaching, while those who considered themselves righteous were shut out because they lacked faith and repentance. This stresses that a true change of heart matters more than outward appearance.
This passage shows us that true faith is not only a promise in words but the fulfillment of that promise in action. God values those who recognize their need to repent and who rely on His grace.
q: In your life, have there been times when your words and your heart did not agree? How can you make sure your actions match your commitment to God?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word the importance of true obedience and repentance. Help us not only make promises with our mouths but show our faithfulness and love for You in our actions. When we stray from the right path, lead us to repent and restore us by Your grace. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Hear another parable. There was a man who was a master of a household, who planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, dug a wine press in it, built a tower, leased it out to farmers, and went into another country.
When the season for the fruit came near, he sent his servants to the farmers, to receive his fruit.
The farmers took his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another.
Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they treated them the same way.
But afterward he sent to them his son, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But the farmers, when they saw the son, said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, and seize his inheritance.’
So they took him, and threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.
When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?”
They told him, “He will miserably destroy those miserable men, and will lease out the vineyard to other farmers, who will give him the fruit in its season.”
Jesus said to them, “Did you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone which the builders rejected was made the head of the corner. This was from the Lord. It is marvelous in our eyes?’
“Therefore I tell you, God’s Kingdom will be taken away from you, and will be given to a nation producing its fruit.
He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust.”
When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he spoke about them.
When they sought to seize him, they feared the multitudes, because they considered him to be a prophet.
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable to reveal the unfaithfulness of Israel's religious leaders and the coming judgment. The landowner in the parable represents God, and the vineyard symbolizes the blessing and mission God gave to Israel. The landowner entrusts the vineyard to tenants (Israel's leaders) and expects to receive fruit at harvest time. But when he sends his servants (the prophets) to collect the fruit that is due, the tenants not only refuse to hand it over but even abuse and kill the servants. Finally the landowner sends his own son (a foreshadowing of Jesus), and the tenants plot to kill him and seize his inheritance.

The point of Jesus' parable is that the Kingdom of God will be taken away from leaders who do not bear fruit and given to a new people who will produce spiritual fruit. This new people points to all believers, including Gentiles, who become part of God's Kingdom through faith in Jesus Christ.

Jesus' words stress responsibility and spiritual fruitfulness. God expects us not only to receive His gifts but also to produce real fruit, which includes a life of righteousness, love, and faithfulness.
q: Which areas of your life need to change so that you may bear more spiritual fruit? How do you view the responsibilities and expectations God has given you?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Jesus Christ's parable the importance of spiritual fruitfulness. Help us be faithful to the mission You have given us and bear fruit that belongs to Your Kingdom in our lives. When we face challenges and trials, give us strength and wisdom to persevere to the end. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.
